summary: The Quran was compiled into a single written mushaf in two stages: Abu Bakr al-Siddiq ؓ ordered the first compilation after the Battle of Yamama (c. 12 AH) to preserve it before more huffaz died in battle; Uthman ibn Affan ؓ ordered the definitive standardised mushaf (c. 25-30 AH) to resolve variant readings spreading across the expanding Muslim world. Both compilations rested on the Quran's preservation in the hearts and the written records of the companions.
narrative:
The Quran was preserved during the Prophet's lifetime ﷺ through two mutually reinforcing channels: oral memorisation and written recording. Scores of companions had memorised the entire Quran — these were the qurra. Simultaneously, whenever Quranic verses were revealed, the Prophet ﷺ would summon scribes (among them Zayd ibn Thabit, Ubayy ibn Kab, Muadh ibn Jabal, and others) and dictate the verses to them, with instructions about placement within surahs. The material was written on whatever was available — flat bones, palm-leaf ribs, pieces of leather, flat stones. What did not exist in the Prophet's lifetime ﷺ was a single bound compilation in one volume, arranged in a single agreed order.

The first compilation was initiated by Umar ibn al-Khattab ؓ, who approached Abu Bakr al-Siddiq ؓ after the Battle of Yamama (11-12 AH) with alarm: approximately seventy hafiz had been killed in that battle alone. Umar feared that if further battles continued to claim memorisers, portions of the Quran could be lost. Abu Bakr ؓ was initially reluctant — 'How can I do something the Prophet ﷺ himself did not do?' — but Umar's reasoning persuaded him. Al-Tabari preserves the account in which Abu Bakr ؓ then summoned Zayd ibn Thabit ؓ, the Prophet's ﷺ own primary scribe, and charged him with the task.

Zayd ibn Thabit ؓ recalled his own initial reluctance, shared Abu Bakr's hesitation, but eventually undertook the task. His methodology — recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari — was rigorous: he gathered every piece of written Quranic material he could find, and cross-referenced everything against the memory of at least two reliable companions for every verse. He accepted no written piece without oral confirmation, and accepted no oral recitation without written corroboration. Ibn Kathir describes this as the most careful process of textual verification in early Islamic history. The resulting compilation — a mushaf kept first with Abu Bakr ؓ, then with Umar ؓ, and then entrusted to Hafsah bint Umar ؓ (one of the Prophet's widows and a hafizah herself) — was the master copy.

The second, definitive compilation came during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan ؓ, approximately 25-30 AH. The immediate trigger was a report from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman ؓ, who had been on campaign in Azerbaijan and Armenia and was alarmed by disagreements among the Muslim soldiers from different regions over the recitation of the Quran. Different companions had memorised the Quran in different dialects (ahruf), and these were being transmitted to new Muslims who had no way to adjudicate between them. Hudhayfa came to Uthman and said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, catch this community before they differ about the Book as the Jews and Christians differed about their scriptures.'

Uthman ؓ recalled Hafsah's ؓ mushaf from the Abu Bakr compilation and appointed a committee of four to prepare a standardised text: Zayd ibn Thabit ؓ (the primary scribe), Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr ؓ, Said ibn al-As ؓ, and Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham ؓ. The committee was instructed that wherever they disagreed on a word or reading, they should write it in the dialect of the Quraysh, since the Quran was revealed in the Qurayshi tongue.

The committee produced multiple copies of the standardised mushaf. Uthman ؓ dispatched one to each of the major garrison cities of the Muslim world — Makkah, Kufa, Basra, Syria, and others — and ordered all variant written copies to be burned. This act was controversial to some, including certain companions who had personal mashufs with marginal notes, but the rationale — to prevent future sectarian divergence on the text — was accepted by the overwhelming majority of companions. The reading of the Quran in the standardised Uthmani rasm is the text recited by the entire Muslim world to this day.

Classical scholarship — including Ibn Abi Dawud al-Sijistani's Kitab al-Masahif and the accounts in al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir — is unanimous that both compilations preserved the Quran with meticulous fidelity. No verse was added or removed; the process was one of standardisation, not composition. The Quran's miraculous preservation across oral, written, and editorial transmission is itself understood as a fulfilment of the divine promise in 15:9: 'Indeed, it is We who sent down the Remembrance and indeed We are its guardian.'
